`JSON.stringify(prev.autoReimbursement) !== JSON.stringify(next.autoReimbursement)` performs a deep serialization comparison when a shallow field-level comparison would be more precise and efficient. The `autoReimbursement` type is `OnyxValueWithOfflineFeedback<{limit?: number}, 'limit'>`, which includes `pendingAction` and `pendingFields` from the `OfflineFeedback` mixin. `JSON.stringify` will detect changes in these offline-feedback metadata fields as "relevant" policy changes, triggering unnecessary report recomputations during optimistic updates when only the pending state flipped -- not the actual `limit` value.

Additionally, `JSON.stringify` is not guaranteed to produce stable key ordering across all JavaScript engines, though in practice V8 and Hermes maintain insertion order.

Compare only the fields that actually affect report badge computation:

```ts
prev.autoReimbursement?.limit !== next.autoReimbursement?.limit
```

Using `deepEqual` for the entire transaction object creates performance overhead that often exceeds the re-render cost. Compare only specific relevant properties.

**Fix**: Use shallow comparison of specific properties:
```tsx
const MemoizedCard = memo(MyCard, (prev, next) => 
    prev.transaction.transactionID === next.transaction.transactionID && 
    prev.onPress === next.onPress
);
```

Deep equality checks recursively compare all nested properties, creating performance overhead that often exceeds the re-render cost they aim to prevent. Using `deepEqual` on `allTransactionDrafts` (an `OnyxCollection<Transaction>`) will compare every property of every transaction in the collection on every render.

Consider comparing only the specific properties or IDs that affect the `actionableItemButtons` behavior:

```tsx
// Instead of deep equality on the entire collection:
Object.keys(prevProps.allTransactionDrafts ?? {}).length === Object.keys(nextProps.allTransactionDrafts ?? {}).length &&
Object.keys(prevProps.allTransactionDrafts ?? {}).every(key => 
    prevProps.allTransactionDrafts?.[key]?.transactionID === nextProps.allTransactionDrafts?.[key]?.transactionID
)
```

Or if only specific transaction IDs matter for the actionable buttons, track just those IDs rather than the entire collection.

Using `deepEqual` on the entire `cardList` object creates performance overhead that likely exceeds the re-render cost it aims to prevent. Deep equality checks recursively compare all nested properties of potentially large data structures.

**Reasoning:**
The `cardList` can contain many cards, and deep equality will traverse all properties of all cards on every render. This is expensive and unnecessary when the component likely only needs to know if a specific card relevant to the current report action has changed.

**Suggested fix:**
Instead of deep comparing the entire `cardList`, compare only the specific card that matters for this report action:

```typescript
// Extract the relevant cardID from props
const prevCardID = prevProps.action?.originalMessage?.cardID;
const nextCardID = nextProps.action?.originalMessage?.cardID;

// Compare specific card if cardID exists
(prevCardID === nextCardID) &&
(\!prevCardID || prevProps.cardList?.[prevCardID] === nextProps.cardList?.[nextCardID])
```

Or better yet, use a selector in the `useOnyx` call to only subscribe to the specific card needed, eliminating the need for this comparison altogether.

Using `deepEqual` for the entire `details` object in `React.memo` creates performance overhead that often exceeds the re-render cost it aims to prevent.

Compare only the specific relevant properties with shallow comparisons:

```tsx
const MemoizedTrapRow = memo(TrapRow, (prevProps, nextProps) => 
    prevProps.details.id === nextProps.details.id &&
    prevProps.details.isActive === nextProps.details.isActive &&
    prevProps.details.label === nextProps.details.label &&
    prevProps.accent.tone === nextProps.accent.tone
);
```

Using `deepEqual` for `reportNameValuePairs` in the React.memo comparison creates performance overhead. Deep equality checks recursively compare all nested properties, which can be more expensive than the re-render they aim to prevent.

Compare only the specific relevant properties instead:

```tsx
prevProps.reportNameValuePairs?.origin === nextProps.reportNameValuePairs?.origin &&
prevProps.reportNameValuePairs?.originalID === nextProps.reportNameValuePairs?.originalID
```

This provides the same optimization benefits with minimal computational cost.

Using `deepEqual(prevProps.transaction, nextProps.transaction)` performs a recursive deep comparison of all transaction properties, which can be more expensive than the re-render it's trying to prevent.

Compare specific relevant transaction properties instead:
```typescript
memo(
    MoneyRequestConfirmationListFooter,
    (prevProps, nextProps) =>
        prevProps.transaction?.receipt === nextProps.transaction?.receipt &&
        prevProps.transaction?.amount === nextProps.transaction?.amount &&
        prevProps.transaction?.merchant === nextProps.transaction?.merchant &&
        // ... other relevant transaction properties
        prevProps.shouldShowTax === nextProps.shouldShowTax &&
        // ... rest of comparisons
);
```

Using `deepEqual` for comparing menuItems creates unnecessary performance overhead. Since menuItems is likely to be a new array reference on each render, this deep comparison will run on every update.

Consider using a reference equality check or memoizing the menuItems in the parent component:

```typescript
prevProps.menuItems === nextProps.menuItems
```
